rationale: A wins because it keeps the facts on a leash. "Monzo's second US attempt skips the license that sank the first one" is a real regulation story with the missing proof named cleanly. B has good bones, but "Monzo posted its first annual profit — then spent it on a second shot at America" invents a money trail the update does not give; that is how a promising angle becomes a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "The widely-held belief this cuts against: challenger banks burn cash, struggle to make money at scale, and have repeatedly failed to crack the US" is plausible, but it is outside the supplied update and needs category proof before it becomes pitchable.
"Both data points landed in the same reporting window" slightly overstates the timing; the update says the profit came "this year" and the US launch is now, not that both broke together.
"Monzo's first profitable year, by the numbers" is smart, but the central number is missing. A admits that, but this angle stays thin until the actual profit figure and scope are on record.
gaps_in_B: "then spent it on a second shot at America" is the big sin. The update gives sequence, not funding causality.
"how the US entry playbook has changed" turns one company workaround into a market trend without evidence. That needs other examples or it should be cut down to a case study.
"renting a banking license" and "borrowed license" are punchy but loose. A regulation reporter will punish sloppy shorthand unless the partner-bank arrangement and deposit setup are named precisely.
"does scale in one market transfer?" is a fair question, but 9 million UK customers alone does not prove a US market-test story without invite numbers, product differentiation, or early traction.
